svg.aria-label: Diagram: AWS Managed Microsoft AD creates a managed Active Directory domain on AWS-managed infrastructure. It can run standalone, with users and groups created directly in it, or it can establish trust relationships with existing domains; in that resource-forest pattern user identities stay in the existing domains while the resource forest manages AWS resources. Directory Service uses a two VPC structure in which the EC2 instances making up the directory run outside the customer's AWS account and are managed by AWS; those instances carry two network adapters, ETH0 as the management adapter outside the account and ETH1 created inside the account, so what the customer receives in their subnet is an interface rather than a server. The management IP range of ETH0 is 198.18.0.0/15, which is also the range a customer VPC may not use, so a slash fifteen of their address space is reserved because of an adapter in an account they cannot see. AD Connector is a directory gateway that caches nothing in the cloud, but it has a one-to-one relationship with each on-premises domain including child domains, cannot be shared with other AWS accounts, is not multi-VPC aware, and does not support Active Directory transitive trusts.
svg.title: The forest holds resources and trusts your domain; the servers are in neither
svg.text: Where your users live is a choice. Where the servers live is not.
AWS Directory Service — “a highly available pair of domain controllers in your Amazon VPC”, read closely.
OPTION A — standalone managed domain
“create new managed AD domains to manage
users, devices, and computers on AWS”
Users and groups created directly in it. No trust,
no on-premises dependency.
An ordinary deployment. Not what most people assume.
OPTION B — resource forest, trusting your domain
“establish resource forests that create trust
relationships with your existing AD domains”
“User identities stay in your existing AD domains”.
The forest holds the AWS resources, not the people.
“operational isolation between environments”
or
And the servers run somewhere you cannot see
“Directory Service uses a two VPC structure. The EC2 instances which make up your directory run outside of
your AWS account, and are managed by AWS.”
ETH0 “the management adapter, and exists outside of your account”
ETH1 “created within your account” → this is what lands in your subnet
Not yours, not in your EC2 console, not something you patch. That is the managed part of a managed service.
Two bullets on one page explain each other, and the page connects neither
YOUR VPC “cannot create … in a VPC using addresses in the 198.18.0.0/15 address space”
THEIR ETH0 “The management IP range of your directory’s ETH0 network is 198.18.0.0/15”
Reading the join is mine, not AWS’s. The effect: a /15 of your space is reserved by an adapter you do not own.
AD Connector: a gateway that stores nothing — and three limits that are not about size
“a directory gateway … without caching any information in the cloud” — which is why a security team accepts it.
1-to-1 with each domain, child domains included · “cannot be shared with other AWS accounts”
“not multi-VPC aware” · no transitive trusts · but “no enforced user or connection limits”
So the count is domains × accounts × VPCs. Organisational shape decides it, not user numbers.
What your VPC commits to, before any of the above.
“At least two subnets … in a different Availability Zone and … of same network type” · “The VPC must have default
hardware tenancy” · an on-premises trust needs forest and domain functional levels at “Windows Server 2003 or higher”.
Every word of “a pair of domain controllers in your VPC” is true, and the sentence still misleads.
